revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Field Day Ribbons
revealWordProblem.text: For Field Day, the PE teacher is ordering award ribbons and pin buttons. Ribbons come in packs of 7 and pin buttons come in packs of 10. She wants to buy the exact same number of ribbons as pin buttons, with none left over, and she wants to buy as few packs as possible. What is the fewest ribbons (and pin buttons) she can buy, and how many packs of each does that require? Explain how the LCM solves this.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The fewest number of ribbons and pin buttons she can buy is the LCM of 7 and 10. Since 7 and 10 share no common factors other than 1, the LCM is their product: LCM(7, 10) = 70. She needs 70 ÷ 7 = 10 packs of ribbons and 70 ÷ 10 = 7 packs of pin buttons, giving exactly 70 of each with none left over.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — What is the least common multiple (LCM)?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: The LCM is the FIRST number that shows up in both numbers' multiple lists — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want the LCM of 4 and 6. I skip count the multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
Then I skip count the multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24.
I look for the first number in BOTH lists. 12 is in both lists, and it comes before 24.
So the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. I check: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so both go into 12 evenly.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Here are the first several multiples of 4 and 6 mixed together. Sort them — which are common multiples of BOTH 4 and 6, and which are multiples of only one? As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

discourse.prompt: What is the least common multiple of 4 and 6? How did sorting the multiples help you find it?
discourse.sentenceFrame: The LCM of 4 and 6 is ___ because it is the smallest number in the ___ group.

onLevel.stem: Two buses leave the station at 8:00 AM. Bus A returns every 15 minutes and Bus B returns every 20 minutes. When is the next time both buses are at the station together?
onLevel.explanation: LCM(15, 20) = 60 minutes. Both buses return together 60 minutes after 8:00 AM, at 9:00 AM.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. LCM(15, 20) = ___ minutes.
40 minutos funciona para el autobús B (40 = 2 × 20), pero 40 no es múltiplo de 15, así que el autobús A todavía no ha vuelto. El momento debe servir para los dos.
80 minutos es múltiplo de 20 pero no de 15. Extiende las dos listas desde el principio y busca la primera vez que coinciden.
hints: Both buses start together at 8:00 — they meet again after a number of minutes that both 15 and 20 divide evenly.
List each bus's return times in minutes and look for the first time that appears in both lists, then add it to 8:00 AM.
Bus A returns at 15, 30, 45, … minutes. Write Bus B's list (20, 40, …) underneath and find the first shared time, then add it to 8:00.
onLevel.stemEs: Dos autobuses salen de la estación a las 8:00 AM. El autobús A regresa cada 15 minutos y el autobús B regresa cada 20 minutos. ¿Cuándo es la próxima vez que los dos autobuses están juntos en la estación?
onLevel.explanationEs: MCM(15, 20) = 60 minutos. Los dos autobuses regresan juntos 60 minutos después de las 8:00 AM, es decir, a las 9:00 AM.

onLevel.title: Spot Maya's Mistake — LCM of 6 and 9

workedExample.label: Choose the answer
workedExample.work: Maya saw that 9 is bigger than 6, so she wrote LCM = 9.

onLevel.correctWork: The LCM is not just the larger number. Check: 9 is in the multiples of 9, but it is NOT in the multiples of 6 (6, 12, 18...). The first number in BOTH lists is 18, so the LCM of 6 and 9 is 18.
hints: Maya picked 9 because it is the larger number. Is 9 a multiple of 6? Skip count: 6, 12, 18 — there is no 9.
The LCM must appear in BOTH multiple lists. Find the smallest number that is in the 6s AND the 9s: 18.
onLevel.titleEs: Encuentra el error de Maya — el m.c.m. de 6 y 9
onLevel.explanation: In the last step Maya chose 9 just because it is the larger number, but 9 never appears in the multiples of 6 (6, 12, 18, 24). The LCM has to be in both lists, and the first number in both is 18, so the LCM of 6 and 9 is 18.
onLevel.explanationEs: En el último paso Maya eligió 9 solo porque es el número mayor, pero 9 nunca aparece entre los múltiplos de 6 (6, 12, 18, 24). El m.c.m. tiene que estar en las dos listas, y el primer número que está en ambas es 18, así que el mínimo común múltiplo de 6 y 9 es 18.

onLevel.title: Find Jaylen's Mistake
onLevel.correctWork: LCM = 24 (the least common multiple is the SMALLEST shared multiple, not just any common multiple)
hints: Jaylen correctly listed the common multiples. Look at Step 5 — did he pick the smallest one?
The LCM is the LEAST (smallest) common multiple. 24 and 48 are both common multiples, but which is smaller?
onLevel.explanation: Jaylen listed the common multiples 24 and 48 correctly, but in the final step he chose 48 instead of the smaller one. LEAST common multiple means the smallest shared multiple, so the answer is 24.
onLevel.explanationEs: Jaylen escribió correctamente los múltiplos comunes 24 y 48, pero en el paso final eligió 48 en lugar del menor. Mínimo común múltiplo significa el múltiplo compartido más pequeño, así que la respuesta es 24.

onLevel.prompt: You are making party favors. Glow sticks come in packs of 10 and bracelets come in packs of 4. What is the fewest of each you can buy so every favor has exactly one glow stick and one bracelet with none left over? Explain how the LCM solves this problem.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: The LCM of 10 and 4 is ___. I need to buy ___ packs of glow sticks and ___ packs of bracelets to get ___ of each. This works because ___.
hints: Every favor needs one of each item, so the totals must match: a number that is a multiple of 10 AND a multiple of 4.
Find LCM(10, 4) by listing multiples, then divide that LCM by 10 and by 4 to count how many packs of each to buy.
Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, … Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, … Keep both lists going until they share a number, then count packs from it.
onLevel.explanation: Every favor uses one glow stick and one bracelet, so the totals must match and be a multiple of both 10 and 4. The LCM of 10 and 4 is 20, so you buy 2 packs of glow sticks (2 × 10 = 20) and 5 packs of bracelets (5 × 4 = 20) and finish with 20 complete favors and nothing left over.
onLevel.explanationEs: Cada recuerdito usa una barra luminosa y una pulsera, así que los totales deben ser iguales y ser múltiplo de 10 y de 4. El m.c.m. de 10 y 4 es 20, así que compras 2 paquetes de barras luminosas (2 × 10 = 20) y 5 paquetes de pulseras (5 × 4 = 20) y terminas con 20 recuerditos completos y nada sobrante.

extending.stem: One machine runs every 4 min, another every 6 min. They just ran together. In how many minutes do they run together again?
extending.explanation: Skip count: multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12; multiples of 6 are 6, 12. The first shared multiple is LCM(4, 6) = 12 minutes.
choiceFeedback: Does both numbers divide into that evenly?
That's a common multiple, but is it the LEAST? Find the smallest one.
6 minutos funciona para la segunda máquina, pero el 4 no cabe exacto en 6. El momento tiene que ser múltiplo de los dos tiempos.
extending.stemEs: Una máquina funciona cada 4 min y otra cada 6 min. Acaban de funcionar juntas. ¿En cuántos minutos vuelven a funcionar juntas?
extending.explanationEs: Cuenta salteado: los múltiplos de 4 son 4, 8, 12; los múltiplos de 6 son 6, 12. El primer múltiplo compartido es MCM(4, 6) = 12 minutos.
hints: They line up again at a time that is a multiple of 4 and also a multiple of 6 — that is the least common multiple.
List the multiples of each number and watch for the first value that shows up in both lists.
Start the lists: 4, 8, ... for the first machine and 6, ... for the second. Keep extending both until the same number appears in each one.
hintsEs: Vuelven a coincidir en un momento que es múltiplo de 4 y también de 6: ese es el mínimo común múltiplo.
Escribe los múltiplos de cada número y busca el primer valor que aparezca en las dos listas.
Empieza las listas: 4, 8, ... para la primera máquina y 6, ... para la segunda. Sigue extendiendo las dos hasta que el mismo número aparezca en ambas.

extending.stem: One ship docks every 8 min, another every 12 min. They just docked together. In how many minutes do they dock together again?
extending.explanation: LCM(8, 12) = 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24; multiples of 12: 12, 24. The first shared multiple is 24 minutes.
choiceFeedback: Does both numbers divide into that evenly?
That's a common multiple, but is it the LEAST? Find the smallest one.
16 es múltiplo de 8, pero no de 12. Sigue extendiendo las dos listas hasta encontrar un número que esté en ambas.
extending.stemEs: Un barco atraca cada 8 min y otro cada 12 min. Acaban de atracar juntos. ¿En cuántos minutos vuelven a atracar juntos?
extending.explanationEs: MCM(8, 12) = 24. Múltiplos de 8: 8, 16, 24; múltiplos de 12: 12, 24. El primer múltiplo compartido es 24 minutos.
hints: Both ships dock together at a time that is a multiple of 8 and also a multiple of 12.
Skip count by each number separately, then look for the first time the two counts land on the same value.
Multiples of 8 begin 8, 16, ... and multiples of 12 begin 12, ... Keep extending both lists until one number turns up in each.
hintsEs: Los dos barcos atracan juntos en un momento que es múltiplo de 8 y también de 12.
Cuenta salteado con cada número por separado y busca la primera vez que los dos conteos caen en el mismo valor.
Los múltiplos de 8 empiezan 8, 16, ... y los de 12 empiezan 12, ... Sigue extendiendo las dos listas hasta que un número aparezca en las dos.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — Crew Member's Schedule Sync Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: The water recycler cycles every 8 minutes and the heat exchanger cycles every 12 minutes. They just ran together. When do they next sync?

workedExample.label: Pick the number to use
workedExample.work: The greatest factor that 8 and 12 share is 4.

extending.correctWork: Step 4 should find the LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE, not the greatest common FACTOR. 'When do repeating events line up?' calls for the LCM. The first multiple in both lists is 24, so they next sync in 24 minutes.
hints: A scavenger-hunt schedule asks WHEN two repeating events meet again — that is an LCM problem, not a GCF problem.
GCF (4) splits things into equal groups; LCM lines up repeating cycles. Look at both multiple lists and find the smallest number that appears in both: 24.
extending.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2 — el error de sincronización de horarios de un tripulante
extending.explanation: Step 4 switched to the greatest common FACTOR (4) instead of the least common MULTIPLE. A question about when two repeating cycles line up again calls for the LCM, and the first number in both lists — 8, 16, 24, 32 and 12, 24, 36 — is 24, so the two systems next sync in 24 minutes.
extending.explanationEs: El paso 4 cambió al máximo común DIVISOR (4) en lugar del mínimo común MÚLTIPLO. Una pregunta sobre cuándo dos ciclos que se repiten vuelven a coincidir requiere el m.c.m., y el primer número que está en las dos listas — 8, 16, 24, 32 y 12, 24, 36 — es 24, así que los dos sistemas se sincronizan de nuevo en 24 minutos.

extending.stem: What is the LCM of 3 and 5?
extending.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ... Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, ... The smallest common multiple is 15.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
5 aparece al contar de 5 en 5, pero no aparece al contar de 3 en 3. Busca un número que esté en las dos listas.
30 sí está en las dos listas, pero no es el más pequeño. Vuelve a las listas y deténte en el primer múltiplo que compartan.
hints: LCM is about MULTIPLES (counting UP by each number), not factors. You want the smallest number BOTH lists reach.
Skip count by 3s in one row and by 5s in another row, then scan for the first number that appears in both rows.
Write the 3s row: 3, 6, 9, 12, … Then start the 5s row: 5, 10, … Stop as soon as one number shows up in both rows.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el MCM (mínimo común múltiplo) de 3 y 5?
extending.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ... Múltiplos de 5: 5, 10, 15, ... El menor múltiplo común es 15.

extending.stem: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?
extending.explanation: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, ... The smallest common multiple is 24.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
Parece que sumaste 6 + 8. El MCM no se obtiene sumando: hay que buscar un número que aparezca en las dos listas de múltiplos.
6 es múltiplo de 6, pero no de 8. Sigue contando de 6 en 6 hasta llegar a un número que también salga al contar de 8 en 8.
hints: Careful: 6 + 8 is not a multiple of either number. You need a number that both 6 AND 8 divide into evenly.
List multiples of the LARGER number, 8, and check each one: is it also divisible by 6? Stop at the first hit.
Test 8: divisible by 6? No. Test 16: divisible by 6? No. Keep climbing the 8s list until a number divides evenly by 6.
extending.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Múltiplos de 8: 8, 16, 24, ... El menor múltiplo común es 24.

extending.stem: What is the LCM of 4 and 10?
extending.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ... Multiples of 10: 10, 20, ... The smallest common multiple is 20.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
10 es múltiplo de 10, pero no de 4. Cuenta de 4 en 4 y fíjate si el 10 aparece en esa lista.
2 es un factor común de los dos números, no un múltiplo común. El MCM nunca puede ser menor que 4 ni que 10.
hints: The LCM is the smallest number both 4 and 10 count into — it is often much smaller than 4 × 10 = 40.
List the multiples of 10 (the bigger number) and test each one for divisibility by 4.
Is 10 divisible by 4? 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, so no. Move up to the next multiple of 10 and run the same test.
extending.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ... Múltiplos de 10: 10, 20, ... El menor múltiplo común es 20.

extending.stem: What is the LCM of 2 and 7?
extending.explanation: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = 14.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you halved the correct amount. Instead: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = ___.
2 es múltiplo de 2, pero no de 7. El MCM nunca puede ser menor que el mayor de los dos números.
Parece que sumaste 2 + 7. El MCM se busca contando múltiplos, no sumando los números.
hints: Notice that 2 and 7 are both prime — they share no common factor. That makes this a special, faster case.
List the multiples of 7 and find the first one that 2 also divides — in other words, the first EVEN multiple of 7.
Test 7: is it even? No. Move to the next multiple of 7 and check evenness again — stop at the first even one.
extending.explanationEs: Como 2 y 7 no comparten factores comunes (son primos entre sí), el MCM = 2 × 7 = 14.

extending.title: Spot Riley's Mistake — LCM of 4 and 6

workedExample.label: Choose the answer
workedExample.work: Riley added the two numbers: 4 + 6 = 10, so LCM = 10.

extending.correctWork: You do NOT add the numbers. The LCM is the first number that appears in BOTH multiple lists. 12 is in the multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12) and in the multiples of 6 (6, 12), so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
hints: Riley added 4 + 6 to get 10. Check: is 10 in both lists of multiples?
The LCM is the FIRST number that shows up in both numbers' multiple lists — look for the smallest number in both: 12.
extending.titleEs: Encuentra el error de Riley — el m.c.m. de 4 y 6
extending.explanation: In the last step Riley added 4 + 6 = 10, but adding does not produce a common multiple — 10 is not even in either list. The LCM is the first number that appears in BOTH lists, and 12 shows up in 4, 8, 12 and in 6, 12, so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
extending.explanationEs: En el último paso Riley sumó 4 + 6 = 10, pero sumar no produce un múltiplo común; de hecho, 10 no aparece en ninguna de las dos listas. El m.c.m. es el primer número que aparece en LAS DOS listas, y 12 aparece en 4, 8, 12 y en 6, 12, así que el mínimo común múltiplo de 4 y 6 es 12.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Least Common Multiple is multiplying the two numbers together instead of listing multiples to find the smallest shared one. For example, for 4 and 6, a student calculates 4 × 6 = 24 and calls that the LCM, but the actual least common multiple is 12 (multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12; multiples of 6: 6, 12 — 12 is the first number that appears in both lists). This shortcut only works when the two numbers share no common factors (like 4 and 9, where the LCM really is 36 = 4 × 9); for numbers like 4 and 6 that share a factor of 2, multiplying overshoots the true LCM. Always list multiples of both numbers and pick the first one that appears in both lists.

connect.scenario: Hot dogs come in packs of 8 and buns come in packs of 6. You want to buy the exact same number of hot dogs and buns with none left over.
connect.promptQuestion: How does the LCM help you figure out the fewest hot dogs and buns to buy so they come out even?
connect.prompt: I need to buy ___ hot dogs and ___ buns because the LCM of 8 and 6 is ___.

check.stem: What is the LCM of 8 and 6?
check.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24… Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24… The first one they share is 24. 48 is a common multiple but not the least.

check.stem: How many packs of hot dogs do you buy?
How many packs of buns do you buy?
check.explanation: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 packs of buns. 3 packs of hot dogs and 4 packs of buns both give 24, so nothing is left over.

connect.modelAnswer: The LCM of 8 and 6 is 24, so you buy 24 hot dogs and 24 buns — 3 packs of hot dogs (3 × 8 = 24) and 4 packs of buns (4 × 6 = 24). That is the smallest order that comes out even.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — What is the LCM of 9 and 12?
exitTicket.explanation: Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36, ... Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, ... The smallest common multiple is 36.
exitTicket.hint: Think through the problem step by step.
choiceFeedback: That's a common multiple, but is it the SMALLEST one they share?
3 is a common factor, not a multiple — you need a shared multiple.
72 is a shared multiple, but look for a smaller one.
hints: LCM means the SMALLEST number that both 9 and 12 count into — think multiples going up, not factors going down.
Skip count by 12s (the bigger number) and test each value for divisibility by 9; stop at the very first hit.
Test 12: 12 ÷ 9 doesn't come out even. Test 24: still no. Keep climbing the 12s list until 9 divides one of them evenly.

parallelPractice.stem: Find the least common multiple of 36 and 60.

steps.prompt: The smallest multiple that 36 and 60 share is ___.

questions.stem: Which pair of numbers has a GCF of 5?
questions.explanation: 15 = 3 × 5, 25 = 5 × 5. Both share the factor 5, and 5 is the largest shared factor.

questions.stem: What is the GCF of 9 and 15?
questions.explanation: Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. The largest common factor is 3.

questions.stem: What is the GCF of 14 and 21?
questions.explanation: Factors of 14: 1, 2, 7, 14. Factors of 21: 1, 3, 7, 21. The largest common factor is 7.

questions.stem: What is the GCF of 8 and 12?
questions.explanation: Factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The largest common factor is 4.
